sources.title: Annual Dajia Mazu pilgrimage sets off

facts.text: Mazu is a sea goddess, and the Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage is described as the largest religious procession in Taiwan.
The pilgrimage starts from Jenn Lann (Zhenlan) Temple in Dajia District, Taichung, and ends back at the same temple.
The pilgrimage lasts nine days and eight nights, and the walkers travel on foot.
The route passes through Taichung, Changhua, Yunlin and Chiayi before returning to Dajia.
News reports give the length of the route as about 340 km; the Ministry of the Interior describes the round trip as about 300 km.
Along the way the procession stops at around 100 temples.
The goddess stays at Fengtian Temple in Xingang, Chiayi, where a birthday celebration for her is held; then the procession turns back toward Dajia.
Each year at the Lantern Festival, the start date and time are decided by throwing a pair of moon-shaped wooden divination blocks before Mazu's statue.
The pilgrimage takes place in the third month of the lunar calendar, around the goddess's birthday.
Mazu's statue is carried in a palanquin, and many believers kneel by the road so that the palanquin can be carried over them, which is believed to bring blessings.
People who live along the route set up food stations and offer free food to the walkers.
Huge crowds join the final part of the walk; in 2026 about 800,000 people filled Dajia for the last stage, and firecrackers and fireworks were set off.
In 2008, the pilgrimage was named an important intangible cultural asset of Taiwan.
The pilgrimage has a history of more than a century; the Dajia temple itself is more than 290 years old.
In 2024, the procession left Jenn Lann Temple at 11 p.m. on April 5, stayed at Fengtian Temple on the nights of April 8 and 9, and returned to Dajia on April 14.
